content: The World Health Organization (WHO) published a guideline in 2016 to provide recommendations for infant feeding practices in areas affected by Zika virus transmission. This guideline aims to assist governments, health ministries, policymakers, and healthcare workers in developing local and national protocols for breastfeeding and infant feeding in the context of Zika virus outbreaks. It also serves as a resource for public communication. Zika virus is a mosquito-borne virus transmitted primarily by Aedes mosquitoes, which also spread diseases like dengue, chikungunya, and yellow fever. There is currently no specific treatment or vaccine for Zika virus infection. The symptoms of Zika virus infection are generally mild and include fever, rash, conjunctivitis, muscle and joint pain, malaise, and headache, lasting 2–7 days. However, the virus has been associated with severe complications, such as microcephaly in infants and Guillain-Barré syndrome in adults. The guideline emphasizes that infants born to mothers with suspected, probable, or confirmed Zika virus infection, or those living in or traveling to areas with ongoing Zika virus transmission, should be fed according to standard infant feeding guidelines. This includes initiating breastfeeding within one hour of birth, exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, and continued breastfeeding alongside the introduction of safe and adequate complementary foods up to two years of age or beyond. The guideline development process followed a rapid advice framework due to the urgent need for guidance during the Zika virus outbreak, while adhering to the WHO's standard procedures for evidence-based guideline development. The process included identifying priority questions, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for dissemination, implementation, and evaluation. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology was used to assess the quality of evidence. A systematic review conducted as part of the guideline development identified limited evidence on the potential transmission of Zika virus through breastfeeding. Three case reports involving mother-infant pairs were reviewed. In these cases, Zika virus RNA was detected in the breast milk of infected mothers, and in one instance, replicative virus particles were identified. However, the evidence was insufficient to confirm transmission of the virus through breastfeeding. The review also highlighted the need for further research on the presence and viability of Zika virus in breast milk and other bodily fluids, as well as the potential protective factors in breast milk. The guideline strongly recommends breastfeeding even in the context of Zika virus transmission, as the benefits of breastfeeding outweigh the potential risks. Mothers should receive skilled support from healthcare workers to initiate and sustain breastfeeding, particularly if they or their infants have suspected or confirmed Zika virus infection. Multidisciplinary teams may be necessary to support infants with feeding difficulties or congenital anomalies, such as microcephaly. The WHO acknowledges the limited evidence available and emphasizes the need for ongoing research to better understand the risks and benefits of breastfeeding in the context of Zika virus outbreaks. The guideline will be updated as new evidence becomes available, with the WHO steering group monitoring developments in this area.
